passages.title: How Do Students Spend Their Time Online?
text: In 2025, the student research club at SMA Nusantara surveyed 400 students about how they use the internet outside school hours. Each student recorded their online activities for one week, and the club calculated the average number of hours per day for each purpose. The results are shown in the chart.

The findings surprised many teachers. On average, students spent seven hours a day online, but only one hour of that time was used for schoolwork. Social media was by far the largest category, followed by watching videos. Several students admitted that they often opened social media apps "just for a minute" and then lost track of time.

The club also asked students how they felt about their internet use. Almost two-thirds said they would like to spend less time on social media, and more than half said that their phones distracted them while doing homework. However, many students also pointed out that some of their video watching was educational, such as tutorials on mathematics or language learning.
Based on these results, the club has proposed a "Focus Hour" campaign, encouraging students to put their phones in another room for one hour every evening while they study.

passages.title: Our School Goes Solar
text: At the end of 2024, SMK Mandiri installed solar panels on the roofs of its workshop and classroom buildings. The project was funded by a partnership between the school, a local energy company, and the parents' association. Students from the electrical engineering department helped with the installation as part of their practical training.

The chart shows the amount of electricity the panels produced each month in 2025. In total, the panels generated about 18,350 kWh during the year, which covered roughly forty percent of the school's electricity use. As a result, the school's electricity bill fell significantly, and the savings are being used to buy new equipment for the workshops.

As expected, production was not the same throughout the year. The panels produced the most electricity in the middle of the year, during the dry season, when skies were clear for long periods. In the rainy months, thick clouds reduced the amount of sunlight reaching the panels.
The school now plans to add batteries so that electricity produced during the day can be stored and used in the evening, when the workshops are used for adult training courses.

passages.title: Jakarta's Plastic Bag Ban: Two Perspectives
text:
Text A (from a city government press release)
Since July 2020, shopping centres, supermarkets, and traditional markets in Jakarta have been prohibited from providing single-use plastic shopping bags. Shoppers are encouraged to bring their own reusable bags. The policy aims to reduce the amount of plastic waste that ends up in rivers, the sea, and the city's landfill. Businesses that do not comply may receive warnings, fines, and, in repeated cases, the suspension of their business permits.

Text B (from a student newspaper)
Our reporters visited three traditional markets in South Jakarta and interviewed 30 vendors. Most vendors in the main market buildings said they now use paper bags or ask customers to bring their own. However, some vendors outside the buildings admitted that they still give plastic bags secretly when customers ask for them, because many shoppers forget to bring a bag. Several vendors also complained that paper bags cost more and tear easily when used for wet products like fish. "I agree with the rule," said one vegetable seller, "but there should be cheap alternatives that really work for us."

passages.title: How Do Students Travel to School?
text: A student council in a senior high school in Surabaya surveyed 500 students about how they usually travel to school. The results are shown in the chart. Motorbikes were the most common choice, used by almost two in five students, while bicycles were the least common.

The council also asked how long the trip takes. Students who walk or cycle live, on average, within two kilometres of the school, and their journeys take about 15 minutes. By contrast, students who use public transport spend an average of 50 minutes travelling each way, mainly because of waiting time and traffic.

Many students who travel by motorbike or car said they would be willing to change if there were safer bicycle lanes and a reliable school shuttle. The council now plans to present the results to the principal and the city government.
